items.title: L10: Reading a promotion role as a whole Success Profile
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A promotion advert is not only a list of Behaviours. Success Profiles allow a role to use any mix of Behaviours, Strengths, Ability, Technical skills and Experience, and the advert states which will be assessed, and how. A typical pattern for an EO or HEO role is that Behaviours are tested at the sift through a written statement, then Behaviours and sometimes Strengths are tested at interview, with an Ability test used earlier for a large field. Technical skills, if listed, are assessed against the stated requirement, for example a professional qualification or a demonstrable skill with a tool. Experience is usually assessed through the application or CV, and the advert will say whether unpaid experience counts. Reading the profile as a whole prevents common misjudgements. A candidate who spends all her effort on Behaviour statements may neglect an Ability test that is the first filter, or a Technical requirement that she cannot show. Another may assume that a lead Behaviour is the only one assessed and then be asked about others at interview. Read the advert for four things: what is assessed at each stage, how many words or minutes you get, what the grade-level wording of each Behaviour is, and what the minimum criteria are. If minimum criteria apply, such as a required qualification, failing them ends the application however strong the statement. Plan your preparation to match the stages: practise tests for the Ability stage, draft statements for the sift and rehearse follow-ups for the interview. Where the advert is unclear, contact the recruitment team before the closing date; they can often clarify what is assessed.

questions.prompt: A promotion advert lists Behaviours, a Technical requirement and an Ability test. Where might a candidate who writes only strong Behaviour statements fall down?

options.text: At the Behaviours, because statements are not assessed at the sift stage
At the Strengths questions, which promotion roles never include
At the offer stage, where pre-employment checks are the only test
At the Ability test or a Technical requirement that filters first

questions.prompt: Which pattern is typical for how elements are assessed across stages?

options.text: Strengths at the sift only, with Behaviours left to a reference
Ability tests only at the offer stage, after the interview
Technical skills judged only by a reference from a manager
Behaviours at sift by statement, then Behaviours and Strengths at interview

questions.prompt: What is the effect of failing a stated minimum criterion, such as a required qualification?

options.text: The application can end, however strong the statement is
It is outweighed if the interview goes well
It reduces the score by a point at the sift
It is ignored for internal candidates

questions.prompt: Which four things should you read for in the advert?

options.text: What is assessed at each stage, the words or minutes available, the level wording and minimum criteria
The closing date, the salary, the location and the working hours of the post
The department's history, its size, its main aims and its stated values
The names of the panel members, their grades and their usual work locations

questions.prompt: What can a candidate do if the advert is unclear about what is assessed?

options.text: Prepare equally for every element and hope to cover it
Wait until the interview to find out what is assessed
Contact the recruitment team before the closing date
Ask a colleague who applied for a different role last year

questions.prompt: A candidate assumes only the lead Behaviour is assessed. What risk does she face?

options.text: Being rejected at the sift for naming too many Behaviours in her statement
Being asked at interview about Behaviours she has no example for
Losing marks because she prepared too much material
Being refused an interview because the lead Behaviour was weak

questions.prompt: How does Experience usually get assessed?

options.text: Through the application or CV; the advert says if unpaid experience counts
By a psychometric test taken online before the sift
By a presentation to the panel at the assessment stage
By a written reference from the current manager and nobody else

questions.prompt: Which preparation plan matches the stages of a typical process?

options.text: Practise tests, draft sift statements and rehearse interview follow-ups
Prepare only for the interview, since the earlier stages move quickly
Write one general statement and submit it to every stage
Wait for the sift result before preparing for anything else

questions.prompt: If a role lists Technical skills, how are they assessed?

options.text: By the score awarded for the Behaviours at the sift or interview
By the panel's general impression of the candidate at the interview
By the length of service in the current grade
Against the stated requirement, such as a qualification or skill

questions.prompt: Why is the grade-level wording of each Behaviour worth reading closely?

options.text: It gives the exact words to copy into your answer to match the advert
It is the same at every grade, so only the name matters
It lists the questions that the panel will ask at interview
It shows the scope and independence expected in your examples

items.title: L10: Reframing evidence from AO to EO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Many candidates moving from AO to EO have good evidence but describe it at AO level. Reframing means choosing a different angle on the same work, not inflating it. Suppose an AO processes claims accurately and helps new starters. Her natural Delivering at Pace example might read: 'I processed 40 claims a day and cleared the backlog.' The reframed version emphasises what an EO would do: planning and coordination. For instance: 'When the backlog reached 300 claims, I analysed which types were oldest, proposed a split of work among four of us according to experience, set a daily target and checked progress each afternoon. After three weeks the backlog was 40.' The facts are the same job in the same team, but the evidence now shows initiative, coordination and judgement. Look for these pointers in your own work: times when you suggested how work should be shared; times when you checked or corrected colleagues' work; times when you were the person others asked; and times when you took decisions beyond the written procedure, within your authority, and could explain them. If you did not do any of those, seek opportunities before applying, such as volunteering to train a new starter or to take the lead on a small improvement. Do not claim to have 'managed' people if you did not; EO evidence is about guiding, not formal management. Good reframing keeps numbers honest, names your own part and shows a decision. Compare a before and after version of an answer and check that the second has more scope, not more adjectives.

questions.prompt: What is meant by reframing evidence?

options.text: Choosing a different angle on the same work to show scope
Adding stronger adjectives to the same facts so that the work sounds bigger
Changing the facts so that they suit the higher grade
Moving the story to a different organisation or setting

questions.prompt: Which version of the backlog answer shows EO-level evidence?

options.text: 'I processed 40 claims a day and cleared the whole backlog by myself in a month.'
'I worked very hard and stayed late for several weeks to clear the backlog.'
'I analysed which claims were oldest, split the work among four of us and checked progress each afternoon.'
'I was always willing to help the team when a backlog built up.'

questions.prompt: Which pointer suggests EO-level evidence in your own work?

options.text: Times when you finished your own tasks early
Times when you followed the procedure exactly
Times when you were the person others asked
Times when you read the latest guidance

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do if she has no EO-style evidence at all?

options.text: Claim to have managed people, since the panel is unlikely to check the claim
Borrow a colleague's example and describe it as hers
Seek chances such as training a new starter or leading a small improvement
Apply anyway with AO examples and explain her potential at interview

questions.prompt: Why should she avoid saying she 'managed' people she did not formally manage?

options.text: Management is never mentioned in the Behaviours for EO roles at all
The word is banned from Civil Service applications
Managers are not allowed to apply for EO posts
EO evidence is about guiding, and the claim may be exposed at interview

questions.prompt: Which feature shows the second version of an answer is genuinely better?

options.text: More words overall, so the answer fills the limit
A longer Situation that explains the setting
A more formal tone throughout the answer
More scope, not more adjectives

questions.prompt: Which decision is acceptable evidence of judgement at EO level?

options.text: A choice that ignores the procedure in order to save the team some time
A choice made without telling a supervisor, to avoid delay
A choice made because it was quicker for the team
A choice within your authority, beyond the procedure, that you can explain

questions.prompt: What does the figure 'backlog fell from 300 to 40 in three weeks' contribute?

options.text: A claim that she alone deserves the credit
An exaggeration that the panel will probably discount as unreliable
A statement of the hours she worked on it
A measured result that supports her claim of coordination

questions.prompt: A colleague writes: 'I helped new starters.' How could she reframe it for EO?

options.text: Add that she helped them often and was available whenever they asked
Describe how she planned their induction and checked they could do the tasks
Add the names of the new starters she helped
Describe how pleasant and cooperative the new starters were to work with

questions.prompt: Why is it important that a reframed answer still 'names your own part'?

options.text: Names are required by the application form
Assessors score what the candidate personally did
The Civil Service Code requires every answer to name the candidate
Panels prefer short answers that name the candidate

items.title: L10: From EO to HEO: what changes in the evidence
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The jump from EO to HEO is often described as the step from doing and guiding to leading and managing. Assessors usually look for three shifts. The first is accountability: a HEO is typically answerable for a team's or area's results, not only for their own work. The second is people management: setting objectives, giving feedback, handling poor performance and developing individuals. The third is managing complexity: handling competing demands, ambiguity and risk, and making decisions that affect other teams. Consider Leadership. An EO answer might describe a time she led a small piece of work and kept colleagues informed. A HEO answer would more likely describe taking a team through a change, handling resistance, and holding people to account for results. For Managing a Quality Service, an EO answer may describe checking colleagues' work. A HEO answer would describe setting a standard, monitoring it with data, finding the cause of a service problem and agreeing action with other teams. A candidate who has not line-managed can still show these shifts through acting up, leading a project, supervising temporary staff, chairing a working group or covering a manager's role. Important cautions: do not describe disciplinary or performance issues in a way that could identify a person, and do not suggest that managing means telling people what to do. Assessors prefer evidence of setting clear expectations, listening to concerns and agreeing improvement. A HEO answer also needs to show the reasoning behind a choice, including options not taken and risks accepted.

questions.prompt: Which is the first of the three shifts from EO to HEO?

options.text: A higher salary and a different set of terms and conditions
A change of department and of working location
Accountability for the results of a team or area
Working more hours than at EO

questions.prompt: Which answer best evidences HEO-level Leadership?

options.text: Taking a team through change, handling resistance and holding people to account
Keeping colleagues informed during a short piece of work that she led
Leading by example in her own work
Offering to help colleagues when they ask

questions.prompt: Which answer best evidences HEO-level Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Checking colleagues' work for errors and correcting them before it goes out
Correcting her own mistakes quickly and recording what happened each time
Answering complaints calmly and accurately and following up with the customer
Setting a standard, monitoring it with data and agreeing action with other teams

questions.prompt: How might a candidate who has never line-managed still show HEO shifts?

options.text: She cannot, because line management is a requirement for these Behaviours
Through acting up, leading a project, chairing a group or covering a manager
By describing her manager's work as if it were her own
By quoting the wording of the job description

questions.prompt: Why should disciplinary or performance matters be described carefully?

options.text: Because performance matters are irrelevant to the Behaviours
Because the Code forbids any mention of them
To avoid identifying a person and to focus on what you did
Because panels dislike hearing about them

questions.prompt: Which approach to managing performance do assessors prefer to see?

options.text: Telling people what to do and checking up on whether they have done it
Reporting under-performance to a manager without discussing it
Setting clear expectations, listening to concerns and agreeing improvement
Avoiding the issue until the formal review

questions.prompt: Which element is expected in a HEO decision story?

options.text: Reasoning that includes options not taken and risks accepted
A statement that the decision was a brave one in the circumstances
A note of who agreed with it and who did not
The length of time the decision took

questions.prompt: What does 'managing complexity' mean?

options.text: Handling competing demands, ambiguity and risk across teams
Working on difficult tasks alone, without needing any guidance from others
Doing many tasks at the same time without dropping any of them
Learning complex procedures quickly so that she can apply them accurately

questions.prompt: An EO-style Leadership answer used for a HEO role is likely to be judged how?

options.text: Excellent, since it shows initiative
Irrelevant to the Behaviour being assessed
Evidence of Strengths, not Behaviours
Relevant, but lacking the accountability and scope expected

questions.prompt: What makes 'telling people what to do' weak HEO evidence?

options.text: It is dishonest, since nobody in a team can be told what to do
It shows control rather than setting expectations
It is too short to be assessed
It leaves out any mention of results

items.title: L10: From HEO to SEO: what changes in the evidence
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: HEO to SEO is a move from managing a team to leading a larger or more complex area, often managing other managers. The evidence should show breadth, strategic thinking and influence across boundaries. Assessors usually look for several features. First, a clear line of sight from your area's work to the department's priorities, and the ability to explain trade-offs. Second, leading through others, which means setting direction, delegating real responsibility and holding managers to account. Third, managing risk and uncertainty, including escalation and honest reporting of problems. Fourth, working with senior stakeholders and, often, external partners. Fifth, shaping and leading change that people may resist, with a sound case, a plan and evidence of adoption. For Communicating and Influencing, SEO evidence might describe preparing a brief for a senior colleague that set out options and a recommendation concisely, and managing a difficult message to a partner. For Developing Self and Others, evidence might show building a pipeline of future managers, handling a serious performance case through due process and sustaining your own development. A frequent weakness is writing an extended HEO answer, with more detail but the same scope. Another is describing the work of the whole team as personal: SEO panels expect delegation. Use 'I' for what you decided and did and 'my team' for what they delivered at your direction. Include what you stopped doing, what you handed on and how you ensured quality without doing it yourself.

questions.prompt: Which feature most distinguishes SEO evidence from HEO evidence?

options.text: Working harder than colleagues and for longer hours each week
Managing the same team for a longer period
Leading through other managers, with breadth and cross-boundary influence
Handling a greater number of cases personally

questions.prompt: A candidate describes the whole team's work as her own. How will an SEO panel see it?

options.text: As a strength that shows personal commitment to the team's work
As evidence of good teamwork
As irrelevant to the Behaviour being assessed
As a weakness, since SEO evidence should show delegation

questions.prompt: Which pair of terms suits describing delegated work accurately?

options.text: 'I' for what you decided, 'my team' for what they delivered
'We' for everything, so that the credit is shared with the team
'I' for everything, to show clear ownership of the whole outcome
'The department' for everything, to stay neutral

questions.prompt: Which example fits SEO-level Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Preparing a concise brief for a senior colleague with options and a recommendation
Writing a clear email in reply to a customer who has complained
Explaining a new process to colleagues at a team meeting
Answering questions from members of the public at a counter

questions.prompt: What does a 'line of sight' to departmental priorities mean?

options.text: Showing how your area's work serves the department's aims, and explaining trade-offs
Being able to find the department's priorities on the intranet
Having a clear plan for your own working day
Knowing the names of senior officials and ministers

questions.prompt: Which Developing Self and Others example suits SEO level?

options.text: Attending a leadership course and sharing the notes with the team
Building a pipeline of future managers and handling a serious performance case fairly
Asking a manager for feedback on her own work once a year
Mentoring a single new starter for the first month of the job

questions.prompt: Which answer shows leading change that people resist?

options.text: Announcing the change and waiting to see how people react to it
Making the change without telling the people affected
Delaying the change until everybody agrees
A sound case, a plan, handling objections and evidence of adoption

questions.prompt: What is a frequent SEO weakness?

options.text: An answer that is too short to be assessed
An extended HEO answer with more detail but the same scope
An answer that contains no numbers
An answer written in the passive voice

questions.prompt: Which element helps show quality without doing the work yourself?

options.text: How many hours you worked each week to keep the team on track
How many people you supervised directly on a daily basis
What you stopped doing, what you handed on and how you checked quality
How many reports you wrote yourself during the period

questions.prompt: Which behaviour is expected when managing risk at SEO level?

options.text: Honest reporting and timely escalation of problems, with options
Resolving every problem quietly before anyone hears of it
Waiting for instructions before acting on a risk
Avoiding risk by not taking new work on

items.title: L10: Rewriting a weak answer step by step
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Improving an answer is easier with a sequence. Take this draft for Making Effective Decisions at EO level: 'We had a problem with the rota because people kept swapping shifts without telling me. I decided to sort it out. I spoke to everyone and we agreed a new way. It worked well and people were happier.' Step one is diagnosis: the Situation is thin, the Task is implied, the Action says almost nothing, 'we' hides the candidate's part, and the Result is a mood. Step two is to supply the Situation briefly with a number: 'In a team of nine, unannounced shift swaps left the counter uncovered twice in a fortnight.' Step three is the Task: 'As the rota coordinator I had to stop gaps without removing flexibility.' Step four is the Action with reasoning: 'I listed the reasons people gave for swapping, compared three options (a fixed rota, a swap request form, and a shared online sheet), judged that a shared sheet kept flexibility while recording changes, discussed it with the team, and trialled it for a month.' Step five is the Result with evidence: 'No gaps in the next four weeks, and two colleagues asked to use the same method for the Friday cover.' Step six is a reflection if space permits: 'I would involve the manager earlier.' The final version is the same incident as the original but now shows weighing of options, consultation, trial and outcome. Each step addressed a specific fault. Avoid the temptation to improve the style first. Fix evidence, then structure, then wording.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in improving the draft?

options.text: Rewrite the first sentence so that it sounds stronger
Diagnose which parts are thin or missing
Add a quotation from a colleague
Cut the draft down to a shorter length

questions.prompt: Which option in the Action best shows decision-making?

options.text: Choosing the first idea that came to mind and trying it out with the team
Comparing three options and judging which kept flexibility and recorded changes
Telling people firmly to stop swapping shifts
Asking a manager to decide which rota to use

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the Task in the improved version?

options.text: 'In a team of nine, unannounced swaps left the counter uncovered twice in a fortnight.'
'I listed the reasons people gave for swapping.'
'As the rota coordinator I had to stop gaps without removing flexibility.'
'The counter had no gaps in the next four weeks.'

questions.prompt: Which part of the improved Result gives evidence?

options.text: People were happier with the new arrangement and said so at the team meeting
It worked well, and the team liked the arrangement a great deal
Everyone agreed that the new sheet was a good idea for the whole team
The counter was covered for four weeks and two colleagues asked for the method

questions.prompt: Why does the original draft hide the candidate's part?

options.text: It is too short to be assessed
It includes numbers that cannot be checked
It uses 'we' throughout the Action
It names the manager who made the decision

questions.prompt: What order of improvement is recommended?

options.text: Fix evidence, then structure, then wording
Fix wording, then structure, then evidence
Fix structure only, since the evidence is fine
Fix the Result only, because it carries the most marks

questions.prompt: Which optional addition would add reflection?

options.text: 'I would involve the manager earlier.'
'The team was friendly and helpful throughout.'
'It was a very busy time for everyone.'
'I am proud of what I achieved.'

questions.prompt: What does the trial for a month add to the Action?

options.text: It tests the idea before committing and generates evidence
It shows she delayed the decision for longer than was necessary
It lengthens the answer so that it fills the limit
It shows the manager's role in the decision

questions.prompt: How does the Situation in the improved version differ from the original?

options.text: It is longer, with more background about the team and the counter
It uses more adjectives to set the scene for the assessor
It names the people involved in the swaps
It gives a size and a consequence in one sentence

questions.prompt: Why is improving style first a mistake?

options.text: Style is not marked in a written statement, so wording is irrelevant
Better wording on thin evidence does not raise the score
Assessors prefer plain language over detail
It lengthens the process of redrafting

items.title: L10: Attribution when the work was shared
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Most real achievements involve other people, and promotion panels expect candidates to describe them honestly. The skill is attribution: stating your own contribution clearly, acknowledging others and avoiding both overclaiming and self-effacement. Overclaiming says 'I redesigned the process' when you drafted one section. Self-effacement says 'I only helped' when you led the planning, which gives the panel nothing to score. A good method is to divide the work into parts and name yours. For instance: 'The project team of five reviewed the complaints process. I led the data analysis, which showed that 60 per cent of complaints concerned delays in two stages. I presented the findings, proposed changes to those two stages and drafted the revised guidance, which the team agreed.' The reader sees the group, the candidate's role and the specific actions. Several practical rules help. Use 'I' for what you did and 'we' only for decisions or actions made jointly. State the size of the group and your role in it. Where you built on others' work, say so. Where outcomes depended on others, say what you contributed, not that you caused everything. Be ready for questions such as 'What would have been different without you?' and 'What did others do?' A strong answer shows generosity without losing clarity. Avoid sharing others' personal details. Equally, avoid blaming a colleague when a group effort went wrong; describe the issue and your response. If the project's result was strong but your part was small, choose another example for this Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which sentence attributes work honestly?

options.text: 'I led the data analysis and drafted the guidance, which the team agreed.'
'I redesigned the whole process for the department on my own.'
'I only helped a bit with the project.'
'The team did everything and I supported them.'

questions.prompt: What is the problem with 'I only helped'?

options.text: It sounds too confident for the panel and may count against the candidate
It is too long for a Behaviour answer, which should be brief
It names the other people involved
It gives the panel nothing to score, even if you led parts of the work

questions.prompt: What is the problem with 'I redesigned the process' when you drafted one section?

options.text: It is too short to be scored
It overclaims
It is a Result rather than an Action
It is too polite to be believed

questions.prompt: When should 'we' be used in an Action?

options.text: In every sentence, to sound modest
Never, because it hides your part
For decisions or actions made jointly
Only in the Result

questions.prompt: Which question tests your contribution at interview?

options.text: 'What would have been different without you?'
'Where in the building did the project take place?'
'When did the project finish in the end?'
'How large was the room where you met?'

questions.prompt: What should you do if your part in a strong project was small?

options.text: Choose another example for this Behaviour
Describe the project as if she had led it
Use the project but say nothing about her part
Ask a colleague who was involved to write the answer

questions.prompt: How should a group failure be described?

options.text: Name the colleague who caused the failure so the panel can follow the story
Describe the issue and your response without blaming a colleague
Leave out the failure and describe only the parts that went well
Say that it was the manager's fault

questions.prompt: Why state the size of the group?

options.text: It shows the size of the budget
It lengthens the answer so that it fills the limit
It shows scale and lets the panel judge your role in it
It is required by the application form

questions.prompt: Which phrase acknowledges others without losing clarity?

options.text: 'The team agreed the findings; I proposed the changes.'
'The team made all the decisions and I took notes.'
'I did everything myself, from the data to the report.'
'Everyone contributed equally to the outcome.'

questions.prompt: Which of these should you avoid sharing about colleagues?

options.text: The tasks they carried out
The size of the group
The result the group achieved
Their personal details

items.title: L10: Evidence from acting up, loans and secondments
items.body: Temporary promotion, often called acting up, and short placements such as loans or secondments can supply strong evidence for the next grade. Acting up means carrying out the duties of a higher grade for a period, often to cover absence or a vacancy. A loan or secondment places you in another team or organisation for a fixed period. These are useful because they put you in situations that your substantive role may not offer: wider responsibility, new stakeholders, a different team culture. To use them well, treat them as evidence sources from the start. Agree objectives with your manager, note the scope of the role, list decisions you took and keep a record of results. When you write about the experience, describe the level of the role and what you did at that level, not simply that you were acting up. For example, 'I acted up as HEO for four months, managing a team of six and setting their objectives' is only a claim; the evidence is what followed: how you ran the team meetings, how you handled a difficult conversation, how you dealt with a missed deadline and what changed. Many departments say that acting-up experience may count but that assessors score the evidence, not the title. Acting up does not guarantee promotion, nor does it replace competition, because permanent appointments are made on merit through fair and open competition. Do not describe an acting-up period as if you had been permanently appointed. Ask for written feedback from the manager at the end, as it provides independent evidence.

questions.prompt: What does 'acting up' mean?

options.text: Being permanently promoted to the higher grade after a competition
Working extra hours at the same grade to cover a colleague
Training new staff in the team
Carrying out the duties of a higher grade for a period

questions.prompt: Why are loans and secondments useful for evidence?

options.text: They guarantee promotion at the end of the period if feedback is good
They put you in situations your own role may not offer
They replace the need to compete for a post
They shorten the application process

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to use an acting-up period as evidence?

options.text: State that you acted up for four months and the grade you covered
Put the higher title in the first sentence of the answer
Copy the higher grade's job description into the answer
Describe what you did at the higher level, such as running meetings

questions.prompt: What do assessors score when you cite acting up?

options.text: The evidence, not the title
The title of the post held
The length of time spent in the post
The department in which it was held

questions.prompt: Does acting up guarantee permanent promotion?

options.text: It does after six months in the post, as a matter of policy
It does not; permanent appointment is by fair and open competition
It does if the feedback received is good
It does if the vacancy is the one being covered

questions.prompt: Why should you agree objectives at the start of an acting-up period?

options.text: To create a record of scope and results to draw on later
To avoid being given extra work during the placement
To satisfy a human resources requirement for every placement
To reduce the amount of work to be done

questions.prompt: What provides independent evidence at the end of a placement?

options.text: Your own summary of what you did
The job title you held
A colleague's opinion given in conversation
Written feedback from the manager

questions.prompt: Which statement would misrepresent an acting-up period?

options.text: Describing the scope of the role and its main duties
Describing your results in the post, with figures where possible
Describing it as if you had been permanently appointed
Describing feedback you received from the manager at the end

questions.prompt: What should you keep a record of during a placement?

options.text: Hours worked each week
Meetings attended
Decisions taken and results
Names of people who attended

questions.prompt: Which phrase is only a claim and not evidence?

options.text: 'I ran weekly team meetings and agreed objectives with six staff.'
'I acted up as HEO for four months.'
'I handled a missed deadline by replanning the work with the team.'
'My manager's feedback cited how I handled a difficult conversation.'

items.title: L10: Sift statements, CVs and reuse across applications
items.body: Civil Service applications for promotion commonly use a combination of a personal statement, answers to Behaviour questions and a CV or work history. Each has a different job. The CV or work history shows what you have done and where, usually listing roles, dates and main responsibilities. It should be accurate and consistent with the rest of the application. The statement shows how well you meet the Behaviours and other criteria, and it is the main source of evidence at the sift. The interview then tests that evidence in depth. If you are applying for several roles, it is tempting to reuse a statement, but that carries risks. First, departments differ in the Behaviours and grade-level wording, so a statement written for one advert may not match another. Second, a statement that does not use the right scale for the grade will under-score. Third, details copied from earlier applications may not match the new role. A sensible approach is to keep a bank of strong examples and adapt them each time: check the Behaviours asked, the word limit and the level, and rewrite the Action and Result to match. Update your CV with recent roles and achievements, and avoid listing duties without outcomes. Do not use the same words for different Behaviours within one application, as this suggests padding. Keep notes of what you wrote, because the interview panel may have your statement in front of them. If your application is unsuccessful, ask for feedback and note what to adjust, since feedback can improve the next one.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of the CV or work history?

options.text: Show what you have done and where, accurately and consistently
Provide the Behaviour evidence that is scored at the sift
Replace the interview stage
Answer the Strengths questions in advance

questions.prompt: What is the main source of Behaviour evidence at the sift?

options.text: The statement or Behaviour answers
The CV or work history

items.title: L10: Evidencing Behaviours in assessment exercises
items.body: At promotion level some selection processes include exercises in addition to interviews. Typical exercises include a written task, a presentation, a case study or an in-tray exercise, sometimes in a group. These exercises are designed to elicit the Behaviours, so the advert's Behaviours tell you what the assessors will be looking for. In a written exercise, for example, they may mark Communicating and Influencing through clarity, structure and tailoring to the reader, and Making Effective Decisions through the quality of the recommendation. In an in-tray exercise they look for Delivering at Pace through prioritisation, and for Managing a Quality Service through accuracy. In a presentation they may assess Communicating and Influencing, Seeing the Big Picture and Leadership. In a group exercise the focus may be Working Together: contributing ideas, listening, building on others' points and helping the group reach an outcome. Common errors include dominating, speaking over others, or saying nothing. A strong approach is to state your assumptions, structure your thinking, ask for clarification when permitted and show how you weigh options. Timing matters, and unfinished exercises often score less than complete but simple ones. Read the brief carefully for constraints such as audience, word count and date. If you require reasonable adjustments, such as extra time or a different format, you should request them in advance through the process stated in the advert, as the department has duties under the Equality Act 2010 to consider them. Practise with a time limit beforehand and ask a colleague for feedback on clarity.

items.title: L10: Fair process, honesty and conflicts of interest
items.source: Civil Service Code and Recruitment Principles, GOV.UK
items.body: Promotion in the Civil Service is governed by the Recruitment Principles, which require selection on merit following fair and open competition. The Civil Service Commission regulates compliance. For candidates, this means that internal and external applicants are assessed against the same criteria, and personal acquaintance should not affect the outcome. For panel members, it means declaring any conflict of interest, such as a close personal relationship with a candidate, and stepping back from assessing that candidate. For candidates, it also means being honest and not seeking improper advantage. Examples of improper conduct include asking a panel member to share confidential information about other candidates, using inside knowledge of interview questions, or having someone else complete an assessment. References and, where applicable, pre-employment checks verify what you have stated, and discovering that information was false can lead to withdrawal of an offer or disciplinary action. If you are asked to act as a referee, give an honest account of the person's work, based on what you know. If you are on a panel and know a candidate, you should declare this to the chair before assessment. If you feel the process has been unfair, you can use the department's feedback and complaints procedure, and in some cases raise it with the Civil Service Commission. These principles protect trust in the process, and following them is part of the integrity and honesty expected of every civil servant. A candidate who understands and values fair process is also showing the Behaviours, particularly Leadership and Making Effective Decisions.

items.title: L10: Learning from an unsuccessful application
items.body: Not every promotion application succeeds, and what a candidate does next shapes the following one. Feedback is the most valuable resource. Most departments offer feedback after sift or interview, often in writing or by phone. Ask for it promptly, ask specific questions and listen without defending yourself. Useful questions include: Which Behaviours were scored highest and lowest? Was the level of my examples right for the grade? Did my answers show enough of my own part? Were my Results specific? Was there anything in my delivery that made the evidence harder to follow? Feedback comes in different forms. A score and a short comment on each Behaviour is common. Treat the scores as a guide, not a judgement of worth. Sort the comments into three groups: evidence problems, such as vague Actions or missing Results; level problems, where the examples were pitched too low; and delivery problems, such as running out of time or rambling. Each group needs a different response. For evidence problems, rewrite your examples using the structure; for level problems, seek stretch work or choose different examples; for delivery problems, practise with timing and mock questions. Keep a record of the feedback and the actions you take. Consider asking a colleague who succeeded at the grade to review your statement. If you disagree with a score, compare the evidence on the page with the level wording before challenging the result; often the gap is real. Resilience is part of the Behaviours: describing how you responded to a setback can itself be good evidence of Developing Self and Others.

items.title: L10: Putting a promotion application together
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A strong promotion application is built over months and assembled with care. A practical timeline helps. Months before: read the Success Profile for the next grade and identify evidence gaps; seek stretch work; keep a log of examples. Weeks before: check the advert for assessed elements, words, minimum criteria and closing date; choose examples for each Behaviour, ensuring a spread of settings and at least one example showing the grade's scale; draft each answer with the structure and the right pronouns; test for level by asking whether a colleague would recognise it as the target grade. Days before: tighten the language, check numbers and sources, ensure each answer matches its Behaviour and avoid reusing the same story; proofread; check the word limits in the system; save a copy. After submitting: prepare for the sift outcome by rereading your statement, and plan interview preparation, including follow-up questions and backups. If you pass the sift, prepare to speak about each example for two to three minutes, with detail about your role, reasoning, results and learning; prepare for strengths questions by reflecting on what energises you; consider how you will respond to probing and to questions on mistakes. At interview, listen to the question, answer it, and avoid making new claims that you cannot support. Afterwards, note what went well and what you would change, and request feedback. Treat the process as a project. The candidate who plans, tests and reflects is demonstrating Delivering at Pace, Making Effective Decisions and Developing Self and Others, which are the very Behaviours being assessed.
